clue.text: Brace for a blow left at finish of gale

parts.note: a coup is a sudden stroke or blow, as in a coup de grâce

indicators.note: the finish of a word is its final letter, here taken from gale

explanation.surface: Someone braces themselves against a gust as a storm finally dies down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brace' looks like a verb about bracing for impact, but it is the noun meaning a pair, as in a brace of pheasants.
explanation.definitionFit: A brace is a pair of things, especially game birds, so it means two together.

clue.text: Whiff nothing of dung-beetle round middle of house

parts.note: nothing is zero, which looks like the letter O

indicators.note: round means the beetle's name wraps around the next piece

parts.note: the dor is an old name for a dung-beetle, a crossword regular

indicators.note: the middle of a five-letter word is its third letter, from house

explanation.surface: A faint smell, nothing to do with a dung-beetle, hangs about the middle of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: DOR is a dung-beetle; 'round' puts it around U, the central letter of 'house', after O for 'nothing'.
explanation.definitionFit: A whiff is a faint smell or scent drifting in the air.

clue.text: In Grampian broadcast there's time for a grouse

indicators.note: In here says the next piece goes inside the rearranged letters
broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters of Grampian are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: A Scottish radio programme from the Grampian region spends some time on a game bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' turns GRAMPIAN into PARMIGAN, and 'In' puts T for 'time' inside it after the P. 'grouse' could be a complaint, but here it is the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The ptarmigan is a grouse of mountain and arctic regions that turns white in winter.

clue.text: Last buckled under — the last to prepare

indicators.note: something buckled is bent out of shape, so the letters of under are twisted
the last of a word is its final letter, here from prepare

explanation.surface: The last person to get ready gives way under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buckled' rearranges UNDER into ENDUR, and 'the last to' takes the final E of 'prepare'. 'Last' is a verb here, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To last is to continue or survive over time, to hold out.

clue.text: Time I'll get locked up in low French gaol

indicators.note: locked up in says the next pieces sit inside the word for low

parts.note: base means low, as in base motives or base metal
the apostrophe is ignored, giving the letters as written

explanation.surface: A prisoner reflects that he will serve time in a grim French jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locked up in' puts the time and I'll pieces inside the word for low, splitting it before its last letter. 'get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was the Paris fortress-prison stormed in 1789 at the start of the Revolution.

clue.text: Cambridge revue that went further than "hair"?

explanation.walkthrough: A fringe is hair cut across the forehead (a 'bang' in American English); going past it means going further than the hair. The revue's cast came from Cambridge and Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1960s satirical show by Cook, Moore, Bennett and Miller was titled thus; read literally, past the fringe means farther than the hair over the forehead.

clue.text: Drew south-eastern docks at first harbouring ship

indicators.note: harbouring means sheltering something inside, so the vessel goes within the other letters

parts.note: a ketch is a two-masted sailing vessel

indicators.note: at first means the opening letter of docks

explanation.surface: An artist made a drawing of the south-eastern docks with a ship moored inside the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'harbouring' puts the vessel between the S and the E of the south-eastern abbreviation, with the D from 'at first' closing the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To have sketched something is to have made a rough drawing of it.

clue.text: To make fit I cut out first strip

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of I cut are put out of order
first takes the opening letter of strip

explanation.surface: A tailor trims a garment so it fits, cutting away the first strip of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges I CUT into ICTU; 'first' takes S from 'strip'. 'To make' is a link. 'fit' looks like an adjective about clothing; it is a sudden attack.
explanation.definitionFit: In medicine an ictus is a stroke or seizure, a sudden attack of illness.

clue.text: In bar, thinly disguised, you'll find Daedalus here

indicators.note: disguised means the letters of bar and thinly appear in a changed form

explanation.surface: A man sits in a pub, thinly disguised, hiding from someone looking for him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disguised' rearranges BAR THINLY. In Greek myth Daedalus built the maze on Crete to hold the Minotaur, and was himself shut up in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Daedalus designed the Cretan maze for King Minos and was later imprisoned there with his son Icarus.

clue.text: Author can only do novel on Spain

indicators.note: novel means new, so can only do is made into a new arrangement

parts.note: E is the international vehicle registration letter for Spain

explanation.surface: A writer says they can only manage a novel set in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book, which suits an author, but it signals that CAN ONLY DO is rearranged; 'on' sets the letter for Spain at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Conan Doyle was the writer who created Sherlock Holmes.

clue.text: S but returns to the east by the underground train

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'S but returns to the east by the underground train': the wordplay is BUT backwards plus E, and the stray leading 'S' fits no parse; the clue looks corrupted, and a search found no clean version.
annotationWithheld.clue: S but returns to the east by the underground train

clue.text: Attempt, so I'm hearing, to spoil one on boat

indicators.note: so I'm hearing says a word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: an attempt is a try
to mar is to spoil or damage
an means one, as in an apple

explanation.surface: Someone, so they hear, tries to wreck one of the boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so I'm hearing' applies only to the attempt, giving its sound spelt differently; 'on' is a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A trimaran is a sailing vessel with three parallel hulls.

clue.text: From broadcast routine he's obtained Cuban vote

indicators.note: From signals that the letters are taken from inside the words broadcast routine

explanation.surface: A politician's regular broadcast wins over the voters of Cuba.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'broadcast routine', straddling the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel Castro took power in Cuba in 1959 and was repeatedly elected its leader.

clue.text: A fictional giant that seems very keen

parts.note: Gog is one of the legendary giants Gog and Magog, whose effigies stand in London's Guildhall

explanation.surface: A giant from a story seems extremely eager.
explanation.walkthrough: Gog and Magog are legendary giants of British folklore, guardians of the City of London. 'that seems' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Agog means eagerly expectant, excited and impatient to see or hear something.

clue.text: He will oppose profits on a troublesome year

parts.note: profits are gains

indicators.note: troublesome suggests disorder, so the letters of year are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone objects to profits made in a difficult year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troublesome' rearranges YEAR into AYER. 'on a' is a link, though 'a' looks as if it should supply a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To gainsay is to contradict or deny, so one who does it is an opponent or objector.

clue.text: Pinero's young rose gathers three round the green

indicators.note: round means the word for three goes around the next piece

parts.note: a trey is a three in cards or dice
a green, as in a village or bowling green, is a lawn

explanation.surface: A young rose bush in a garden play has three plants set around the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Wing Pinero's 1898 comedy 'Trelawny of the Wells' has a young actress, Rose, as its heroine; 'rose' is her name, not the flower. 'gathers' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose Trelawny is the young actress at the centre of Pinero's play Trelawny of the Wells.

clue.text: Feet of a girl with vermin we hear

indicators.note: we hear says the words are taken by sound

parts.note: a girl's name, Anna, followed by pests, a word for vermin

explanation.surface: A girl's feet are crawling with vermin, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'Anna pests' gives the answer. 'Feet' are units of metre in verse, not body parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Anapaests are metrical units in poetry made of two short syllables then one long one.

clue.text: Region where one-time princess gets severe

parts.note: Di is Diana, the late Princess of Wales
severe means strict

explanation.surface: A place where a former princess turns stern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'where' and 'gets' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A district is an area or zone marked out for administration or by its character.

clue.text: Loud sound that is made by a person of note

explanation.walkthrough: Both readings join with 'that is made by', making it seem a din comes from an important figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a large din; as slang, an important figure, a bigwig.

clue.text: Long for a child and start to emote

indicators.note: start to means the opening letter of emote

explanation.surface: A woman yearns for a baby and starts to show her feelings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' and 'and' are links. 'Long' is the verb meaning to yearn, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache for something is to yearn or pine for it.

clue.text: Work I consumed, that's called "sugar" or "snow"

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
consumed means ate

explanation.surface: A person admits eating something called sugar or snow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sugar' and 'snow' are street slang for heroin and cocaine, hence a narcotic. 'that's called' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar and snow are old slang for hard drugs, and an opiate is a narcotic drug.

clue.text: Accompany English king captured by Scot

indicators.note: captured by says the king's letter is held inside the next word

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A Scotsman seizes an English monarch while escorting him.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside SCOT as SC-R-OT, after E. The surface recalls the Anglo-Scottish wars.
explanation.definitionFit: To escort someone is to accompany them, as a guard or companion.

clue.text: Poem in progress, where we'll see a show

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
on means happening or in progress, as in the game is on

explanation.surface: A poem is being performed at a venue putting on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: The Odeon is a British cinema chain, so it is where one goes to watch a film.
explanation.definitionFit: The Odeon chain runs cinemas, places where films are screened.

clue.text: Put back a snooker ball, holding the spot

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the ball's colour wraps around the next piece

parts.note: the reds are the fifteen red balls in snooker
a spot is a place or location

explanation.surface: A snooker referee returns a ball to its spot on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker, potted coloured balls are put back on their spots, so 'spot' looks like part of the game rather than a plain word for a location.
explanation.definitionFit: Replaced means returned to where it was, restored to its position.

clue.text: You set about chaps turning up for the foe

indicators.note: turning up in a down clue means the letters are read from the bottom upward
set about here means placed around, so the old word for you encloses the next piece

parts.note: ye is an old word for you
chaps are men

explanation.surface: You attack some men who come along, treating them as an adversary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set about' looks like 'attack' but means placed around; 'turning up' then reads the result YMENE upwards in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: An enemy is an adversary or opponent.

clue.text: Fictional governess runs in to see

indicators.note: in says the runs letter goes inside the word for see

parts.note: to see is to eye
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A governess in a novel hurries in to have a look.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside EYE. Jane Eyre is the governess heroine of Charlotte Brontë's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Eyre, title character of Brontë's novel, works as a governess at Thornfield Hall.

clue.text: One Scots town embracing an Ulster MP

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the other words wrap around the next piece

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
Paisley is a town in Renfrewshire, west of Glasgow

explanation.surface: A Scottish town takes in a Northern Irish politician.
explanation.walkthrough: Paisley is a Scottish town near Glasgow; Ian Paisley was the Democratic Unionist leader and MP for North Antrim.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Paisley was the long-serving Democratic Unionist Member of Parliament for North Antrim in Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Fair beast caught in trap? No, just the opposite of both!

indicators.note: caught in, reversed by the clue's last words, puts the trap inside the beast

parts.note: a brute is a beast
a net is a trap for animals

explanation.surface: A fair-haired animal snared in a trap, said to be quite the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No, just the opposite of both!' flips both halves: the opposite of fair (blonde) is dark-haired, and instead of the beast going inside the trap, the trap goes inside the beast.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer means a dark-haired person, the opposite of a fair or blonde one.

clue.text: Eg in a letter are pieces of prose

indicators.note: in says the word for eg sits inside the letter's name

parts.note: ess is the spelt-out name of the letter S
eg means for example, which is also say, as in say, ten pounds

explanation.surface: Examples in a letter make up written pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter is spelt out as a word rather than given as a single letter. 'are' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Essays are short written compositions on a subject, prose works.
